This cold email lead generation case study from Australia shows how we contacted 13,000 prospects in three months for an Australian Google and Meta ads agency, earning 398 replies and 20 sales opportunities. The whole campaign ran on the Instantly cold email platform. 41,400 Emails sent 13,000 Prospects contacted 398 Replies received 20 Sales opportunities The Challenge Our client is an Australian full-service digital agency built around paid advertising: Google Ads and Meta Ads, plus the work that makes ads convert, including web design, conversion rate optimisation and email marketing. Its clients are ecommerce and DTC brands and service businesses that rely on ads for leads. Like most agencies, new business came mainly from referrals and word of mouth. The founders wanted a steady flow of sales conversations with business owners who already invest in advertising, without hiring someone to prospect full time. Our Strategy 1. A Focused Target List We built the list around businesses that look like the agency’s best clients: ecommerce and DTC brands and lead-driven service businesses. At smaller companies we went straight to founders and owners; at larger ones, to marketing and growth leaders with budget authority. Every contact was verified before entering a sequence. 2. Proof-Led Messaging Business owners hear “we’ll grow your business” from agencies every week. Our copy led with the agency’s own proof instead: the brands it has scaled, the ad spend it manages each month, and a low-effort next step in the form of a free marketing plan. 3. More New Prospects, Fewer Follow-Ups Compared with the previous quarter, we moved sending volume away from long follow-up chains and toward fresh prospects. Total emails fell 24.3% while new prospects in sequence rose 24.5%, which kept inbox volume healthy and put more new names in front of the copy that was working. 4. Sending on Instantly All sequences ran on Instantly. We used it to manage sending across the campaign’s inboxes, schedule follow-ups, and track every reply in one place. The numbers in this case study come straight from the campaign’s Instantly analytics. 5. Reply Handling and Hand-Off Every reply was read and classified. Positive replies went to the client as opportunities with the full email thread attached, so the agency’s team picked up conversations that were already warm. The Results Cold email funnel (last 3 months) Prospects contacted 13,000 Unique prospects who started the sequence Replies 398 3.06% of prospects replied Positive replies 20 5.03% of replies were positive Sales opportunities 20 Every positive reply became an opportunity Hover over a stage to see its conversion rate. Metric Result Platform Instantly Campaign Period 3 months Emails Sent 41,400 Prospects Contacted 13,000 Replies Received 398 Reply Rate 3.06% Positive Replies 20 Positive Reply Rate (of replies) 5.03% Sales Opportunities 20 Estimated Pipeline Value $20K Compared with the previous 3 months ▲ +233.3% Opportunities From 6 to 20 sales opportunities, more than three times the previous quarter. ▲ +97.7% Positive reply rate Almost double the share of replies that were interested. ▲ +35.5% Reply rate Better targeting and copy lifted replies per prospect. ▼ -24.3% Emails sent Fewer follow-ups per prospect, more new prospects reached. Hover over a card for detail. The headline number is efficiency. The campaign sent 24% fewer emails than the previous quarter and produced more than three times the opportunities. Better targeting and sharper copy did the work, not extra volume. Cold Email Lead Generation in Australia: Key Takeaways The main lesson from this cold email case study is that selling agency services by cold email is hard, because almost every business owner has been pitched by an agency before. It still works when the message carries the agency’s own proof, speaks to businesses that already spend on ads, and asks for something small. The same approach works for any agency selling services to businesses. See how our AI-powered cold email service works, read about lead generation for marketing agencies , or compare our pricing . Staying Compliant with Australia’s Spam Act Cold email to Australian businesses is governed by the Spam Act 2003. Commercial emails need consent, which can be inferred when a business address is conspicuously published and the message is relevant to the recipient’s role. Every email must also identify the sender and include a working unsubscribe option, with requests honoured within five business days. Targeting by role and keeping messages relevant matter for compliance as well as for reply rates. For another Australian campaign, see how we generated 20 positive conversations with fire-safety decision-makers across all seven states. Common Questions How many opportunities did this cold email campaign generate? 20 sales opportunities in three months, from 13,000 prospects contacted and 398 replies, with an estimated pipeline value of $20K. What reply rate did the campaign achieve? 3.06% of prospects replied, up 35.5% on the previous quarter. 5.03% of those replies were positive, and every positive reply was passed to the client as an opportunity. Who did the campaign target? Founders and owners of ecommerce brands and service businesses that rely on paid ads, plus marketing and growth leaders at larger companies. Which cold email platform did the campaign use? Instantly. Sequences, sending and reply tracking all ran on the Instantly platform, and the results shown here come from its campaign analytics. What does Digital Symantec handle in a cold email campaign? We build and verify the prospect list, write the copy, set up and manage sending, read and classify every reply, and hand positive replies to your team with full context. Is cold email legal in Australia? Yes, when it follows the Spam Act 2003. Messages need express or inferred consent, must identify the sender, and must include a functional unsubscribe that is honoured within five business days. Inferred consent generally covers business addresses that are conspicuously published, where the message relates to the recipient’s role. page.text: The B2B SaaS Outbound Playbook We Ran at Rippling (0 to $10M in Australia) | Outbounda Outbounda How it works Results Blog FAQ Book a Call Outbound 22 September 2026 7 min read The B2B SaaS Outbound Playbook We Ran at Rippling (0 to $10M in Australia) The full outbound playbook behind Rippling's Australian launch, from list building and cold call blocks to the direct mail and partner motions that ran alongside the phone. Matty Morgan Founder, Outbounda If you re looking for a B2B SaaS outbound playbook that actually got used, this is the one I ran as Rippling s first go-to-market sales development hire in Australia. Rippling is a $16 billion HR and payroll business. When we launched here there were four of us in a co-working space in Sydney and nobody in the local HR or payroll market had heard of us. Australia went from zero to $10 million. I m not going to pretend I did that by myself. There was a big inbound channel and a partner network selling behind us. But running cold outbound was my entire job, and it brought in over $7 million in pipeline and over a million dollars in closed-won revenue. Here s what the playbook actually looked like. The playbook from head office didn t work here The assumption baked into the US playbook was that Australian buyers cared about the same things American buyers did. They didn t. Australian businesses have their own payroll legislation and compliance obligations. Budget cycles ran differently. The competitor set was completely different. And the wording that landed in an American email did nothing for a buyer in Sydney. We were also up against an incumbent everyone trusted. Employment Hero is the Australian all-in-one HR system and nearly every company we called was already on it. HiBob had been selling here for a couple of years before we showed up. And the week we opened the Sydney office, the founder of Employment Hero gave an interview to the Australian press saying you can t just drop an American HR and payroll system into Australia and expect it to work. So the biggest player in the market was actively telling buyers not to trust us. Your reps are your market research team We had a messaging problem and no way to solve it from a desk. No analyst report was going to fix it. Our marketing team had never sold into this market. The only source of truth was the calls we were already making. Every week, Noah Adelstein, the head of growth for the region, sat down with us and asked the same three questions: What are you hearing from our prospects? What do they care about? What are they saying about our competitors? Whatever came out of that went straight into the next email sequence, the cold call scripts and the marketing. Then we did it again the following week. Modern awards is the example I always give. Australia has a whole system of industry-specific pay rules, and Rippling had no visibility of it coming in. We only learned how much it mattered because prospects kept raising it on calls. Within weeks it was shaping how we talked about compliance. If you have reps dialling right now, you are already running the most expensive market research programme in your company. Most teams just never collect the results. Book 30 minutes a week and ask those three questions. Build the list around buying signals Knowing what to say only matters if you re saying it to the right companies. I ran LinkedIn Sales Navigator connected directly to Salesforce, so every account I owned showed up inside it automatically. Then I built saved searches for the three things that told me a company might be in the market right now. New leadership in the buying seat A new head of HR or head of people and culture starting somewhere. More often than not, that person is evaluating the systems they ve just inherited. Hiring activity A company with a stack of open roles, especially roles that had been open for months. That told me the business was growing and about to start feeling the pain of running everything on separate systems. Hiring in another country We sold global payroll. The second a company posted a role in another country, they had a problem to solve about paying those people. Signals tell you who to call first. They don t fill a week. You run out of them fast. So on top of the signal accounts I worked through 50 to 100 companies a week whether they d shown me anything or not. Volume negates luck every single time, and the best reps I ve seen are the ones making the calls nobody else wants to make. The list mistake I d undo If I could change one thing, it wouldn t be the script. It d be which companies went on the list in the first place. A huge share of Australian small and mid-sized businesses run payroll through Xero. Back then we had no Xero integration, and our payroll product couldn t handle some of the local compliance requirements yet. We called them anyway. They d take the meeting, take the second meeting, sit through a demo. Then late in the cycle someone would ask how we integrate with Xero, and the deal would die. Every hour spent there was an hour not spent on the part of the market we could actually serve. Build the list of companies you can t win before you build the list of the ones you want. Never call one person at an account Rippling sold HR, payroll and IT device management in a single platform. So I worked backwards from the product: three departments in any given company could care about what we sold. HR — head of HR, people and culture manager, people operations, talent acquisition Finance — CFO, financial controller, finance manager, head of accounting IT — head of IT, IT operations manager That s 10 to 12 people in one business. One person telling me no never took the company off the list. What I said changed with seniority. With a CFO it came down to three things: risk, cost and revenue, and a business case for what happens if the problem never gets fixed. A level or two down, the person is stuck in the weeds with it every day, so with a finance manager I d talk about the manual work and how slow the current system is to use. Two people in the same company will take the meeting for completely different reasons. Even a no is worth something. I once called a financial controller with zero interest in meeting who still told me when their renewal was, what systems they were running and what had gone wrong with them. I called the finance manager at the same company next and opened with it. That isn t a cold call anymore. Protect the calling block My minimum was 100 dials a day. We didn t have parallel dialers back then, so every one of those was me dialling the number myself. My manager Ron had a rule he called 20 before 10 . Twenty dials before 10am, every day. I d be in at 8:30, and by the time most of the team had made their first call I was already 20 deep. I ran the day in blocks so calling had its own protected time. 8:30 to 10:30 non-stop, short break, listen back to a few calls, then straight into the next block. Anything that wasn t calling, like list building and research, was done the day before or handled inside those saved searches. Everyone I found went into Outreach, which told me each morning exactly who to call. Those emails weren t there to book the meeting. They were there so my name wasn t completely unfamiliar when the phone rang. A buyer used to get about five cold emails a day. They re now getting 20 to 30, and most of them read identically because they re written with the same handful of AI tools. The three motions that ran alongside the phone Cold calling brought in most of our meetings. Three other things ran beside it, and all three were doing the same job: making us look like we d been in the market longer than we had. Getting in a room. We hosted private dinners for HR and finance leaders in Sydney and Melbourne, and sponsored the major HR and payroll events. Nobody signed on the night. The point was that the next time we called that company, they d heard of us. Direct mail. Each SDR nominated around 20 accounts a month for a good bottle of wine and a handwritten note. Nothing random about the picks: strong fit on size and industry, or someone who d already shown interest, visited the site or looked us up on G2. Between 70 and 80% of those accounts became a qualified opportunity, and plenty closed. Partnerships. After the SDR role I moved into a channel account executive seat, working with the HR consultants and accountants advising the businesses we wanted. There was no Australian playbook for it, so we built it from scratch. Lunches, sales material, a cut of any referral they sent our way. By the time we spoke to those companies, someone they already trusted had put in a good word. What to take from it None of this is complicated. It s a list built on signals, enough volume underneath it to survive the weeks where the signals dry up, multiple people worked at every account, a protected block of time for the phone, and a weekly loop that turns what your reps hear into what your reps say. The expensive part is the months of calls it takes to work out what actually resonates in your market. That s the bit you can shortcut. Want this running for your company? We build and run the outbound engine: cold email, LinkedIn, and cold calling. You focus on closing. page.text: Does Cold Outreach Still Work | David Eid ← All Articles Marketing Growth 23 August 2026 3 min read Does Cold Outreach Still Work It works, and worse than it used to, and better than the people who quit it think. What has changed and what a sane version looks like now. Cold outreach still works. It is harder than it was, the volume game is finished, and the people declaring it dead are usually the ones who were only ever doing the version that died. Two things changed and neither of them was the channel. What actually changed Inboxes got defended properly. Sending infrastructure now gets judged on engagement, not just on volume and authentication, so a campaign that nobody opens quietly stops reaching anyone at all. You are not blocked. You are just filed somewhere nobody looks. And the recipient has seen the pattern. The fake personalisation, the first line about their recent post, the "just circling back" on a thread they never replied to. Every one of those is now a signal that this is automated, and the response is instant deletion. Generative tools made that worse, not better. Everyone got the same ability to sound personal at scale, so sounding personal at scale stopped meaning anything. What still works Small volume, real research. Twenty a week where you have actually looked at the business beats a thousand where a tool filled in a variable. That ratio is uncomfortable for anyone who liked the old maths, and it is the trade. A specific observation. Not "I loved your website." Something that proves you looked. You are ranking third for a term where the two above you have thinner pages. Your enquiry form asks for eleven fields. Your best case study is buried three clicks deep. That opening earns a reply because it already gave something. A small ask. The gap between a cold email and a fifty thousand dollar engagement is too wide to close in one message. Ask for a reply, not a meeting. Ask a question they can answer in one line. Warm-adjacent targeting. People who follow you, who have visited the site, who share a connection, who commented on something in your space. Barely warmer, and the response rate difference is large. The thing that changes the economics entirely Outreach works dramatically better when the person already knows your name. If they have seen you in their feed for three months, your email is not cold. It is a follow-up to a relationship that has been running one way. Reply rates on that are a different sport. That is the real argument for building an audience before you need one. It does not replace outreach, it makes every outreach message land differently, and it is why we push organic first with every business we work with. Ten warm inbound conversations a day is what a personal brand produces at scale, and the outreach that runs alongside it converts at a rate the same message could never hit alone. What to stop doing Buying enormous lists. Sending from your primary domain. Following up six times on silence. Opening with a compliment. Attaching a deck. Asking for thirty minutes in the first message. The honest maths Small volume, real research, a specific observation and a small ask will produce a modest number of replies from a modest number of sends. That is not a failure, it is the actual conversion rate of the channel now, and a handful of real conversations a week is a functioning pipeline for most service businesses. The mistake is measuring it against the numbers that worked in 2019 and concluding the channel is dead, when what died was the version of it that required no effort. Nobody has opened it since the day it was set up, or the owner has it bookmarked and reads the average position column like a league table, twice a day, worrying about a number that moves for reasons they cannot influence. Table of Contents Toggle What Search Console Is, and Who It Is For What it reports on, and what it cannot see Why it is not Google Analytics Setting It Up Properly on a WordPress Site Domain property versus URL prefix Verifying ownership and adding users The Five Reports Worth Your Attention Performance: queries, pages and countries Page Indexing: what the states really mean Sitemaps, Core Web Vitals and Links Reading the Performance Report Without Panicking Clicks, impressions, CTR and average position Why your rank tracking tool disagrees with Google Diagnosing a Page That Will Not Index URL Inspection and the live test Requesting indexing the right way Alerts, Manual Actions and Security Issues A Monthly 20 Minute Routine The three questions to answer each month What to export and keep Mistakes That Make Search Console Useless What to Do When the Numbers Fall Search Console FAQ Do I need Search Console if my developer already set it up? How often should I check it? Why does my position look worse in Search Console than in my rank tracker? What does it mean when a page says it is discovered but not indexed? Can Search Console tell me if I have been penalised? What should I export and keep? Get a free consultation with us Both are easy to understand. It is free, it is the only place Google reports its own data about your site, and it becomes genuinely useful once you know which four or five screens matter and what the numbers cannot tell you. After 13 years of working with it, my view has settled. Google Search Console is a diagnostic instrument, not a scoreboard, and most of it can be ignored most weeks. What follows is what to set up, what to read, what to leave alone, and a monthly routine that takes about twenty minutes. What Search Console Is, and Who It Is For What it reports on, and what it cannot see Google describes the service in one line: "Search Console provides information on how Google crawls, indexes, and serves websites." That framing tells you which questions the tool can answer. Whether a page is indexed. Whether Google hit an error fetching it. Which queries returned your pages in results. Whether any manual action or security problem exists. What it cannot see is everything that happens after the click. No revenue, no form submissions, no behaviour on the page, no attribution. Those are analytics questions, and expecting search reports to answer them is the root of most disappointment with the tool. Why it is not Google Analytics The two get confused at least once in every project. Search Console reports on Google's side of the transaction: what it crawled, what it kept, and what it served for which query. Analytics reports on your side: what happened after someone arrived. One tells you whether you were shown, the other tells you what the visit was worth. Setting It Up Properly on a WordPress Site Domain property versus URL prefix A domain property covers every version of your site: secure and unsecured, www and non www, and every subdomain. A URL prefix property covers one address pattern only. Choose the domain property. Otherwise half your reporting lives somewhere else and you spend a month wondering why part of the site is missing from the numbers. Verifying ownership and adding users Verification through a DNS record or an uploaded file both work, and the choice matters less than who holds access afterwards. Ask for your own user with full permission. If a developer or agency holds the only verified property and you have no login, fixing that is the first task, ahead of any reporting question. The Five Reports Worth Your Attention Performance: queries, pages and countries The Performance report shows what your pages were served for, and Google describes the default window plainly: "The default view of the report shows click and impression data for your site in Google Search results for the past three months." Read it by query first, then by page, then narrow the date range when you want to investigate something specific. Page Indexing: what the states really mean The Page Indexing report groups addresses by state: indexed, crawled but not indexed, discovered but not indexed, alternate page with a proper canonical, and several more. Read the states as a queue of decisions running from discovery down to confirmation. A page sitting in discovered but not indexed has a different problem from one sitting in crawled but not indexed, and the fixes are not interchangeable. Sitemaps, Core Web Vitals and Links The remaining reports are useful on the days you need them and quiet the rest of the time. Sitemaps tells you whether the file was read and how many addresses were accepted. Core Web Vitals groups page experience problems. Links shows what Google sees pointing at your site, internal and external, which is occasionally revealing when an internal link you expected is not being counted. Reading the Performance Report Without Panicking Clicks, impressions, CTR and average position Four numbers and one habit. Clicks are visits from search. Impressions are how often you appeared. The ratio between them is your click through rate. Average position is the mean rank of your topmost result across every query and location where you appeared, which is why it can look worse in a month when traffic actually grew. Why your rank tracking tool disagrees with Google Because they measure different things. Google explains one reason clearly: "Even if a query appears in your list, you might not see your site in results if you run the same query in Google Search. This is because Search results are specific to the time, place, device, and recent history of the person searching." A rank tracker checks one query, from one location, on a schedule. Treat the two as instruments rather than verdicts. The full detail sits on the Performance report help page . Diagnosing a Page That Will Not Index URL Inspection and the live test URL Inspection is the workhorse. Google describes it as the tool that "provides information about Google's indexed version of a specific page, and also allows you to test whether a URL might be indexable." Use the live test after a fix, so you are comparing against what exists now rather than what Google last saw. Requesting indexing the right way One request after a real change, then patience. Google also names the limit of the tool: "The URL Inspection tool doesn't take into account all requirements for appearing on Google." A page can be perfectly indexable and still never appear for the query you care about, because indexability and relevance are separate tests. Both are covered on the URL Inspection help page . Alerts, Manual Actions and Security Issues Check these three on your first visit and monthly afterwards. Manual actions are rare and always explicit, naming the reason and the affected section. Security issues flag hacked content, malicious redirects and unwanted software, and they are worth acting on the day they appear. Beyond the reports, Search Console sends email when it finds something, and those messages are one of the few notifications from Google worth keeping switched on. Both reports are the definitive answer to the question owners ask most often after a bad month. If a penalty exists, it appears here with a description. If nothing appears here, the cause is elsewhere. A Monthly 20 Minute Routine The three questions to answer each month Did more of the right people find us, judged by clicks and impressions on the queries that matter commercially. Did anything break, judged by the Page Indexing report and the error counts. And what changed, judged by comparing this month with the same month last year rather than with last month. Those three questions take less time than scrolling the interface randomly, and they produce a decision rather than a feeling. What to export and keep Export the Performance report by query and by page, and note the indexed and excluded address counts. The interface keeps a limited window, so two or three quarters of exported history is the only dependable way to tell whether a change helped. Once you have that export habit, the next step is usually joining it to the behaviour data, which is when you need the analytics layer as well . Mistakes That Make Search Console Useless Four mistakes do most of the damage. Checking daily and reacting to incomplete data. Reading average position as a score rather than an average. Comparing a thirty day period with a ninety day period and drawing a conclusion. And treating the tool as a submission queue rather than a report. Google's own advice on frequency is the plainest sentence in the documentation: "There is no need to sign in to the tool every day." Its guidance adds that a monthly check, or a check after site changes, is enough. One more fact catches people out. The removals tool is temporary rather than permanent, because "a successful request lasts only about six months, to allow time for you to find a solution to either allow the content to be seen or to remove it permanently." If you need a page gone for good, the temporary request is not the mechanism. The whole picture is on Google's page about getting started with Search Console . What to Do When the Numbers Fall Work through a short order. Check Manual Actions and Security Issues first, because they are definitive. Then check the Page Indexing report for a fall in indexed addresses. Then check whether an address pattern changed, including a redirect that stopped resolving or a template edit that added a noindex instruction. Then look at the queries themselves, because a fall in brand queries and a fall in non brand queries mean different things. If the reports are clean and the queries moved, the cause is usually competitive or intent related rather than technical. Two habits make all of this quicker. Keep the technical SEO checklist this feeds into beside the account, and read the reports with a consultant to read it with you at least once a quarter. If you are starting from scratch, the questions owners ask about Search Console cover the setup problems that come up most. Search Console FAQ Do I need Search Console if my developer already set it up? Yes, and you should hold your own access. Google describes it as a free service that helps you monitor, maintain and troubleshoot your site's presence in search, and it is the only place that reports Google's own data about your property. If your developer or agency owns the only verified property, ask to be added before anything else happens. How often should I check it? Google's own guidance is that there is no need to sign in every day, and that a monthly check, or a check after site changes, is enough. Weekly is reasonable if you are publishing actively. Daily checking mostly produces worry, because the newest data is incomplete and average position moves for reasons outside your control. Why does my position look worse in Search Console than in my rank tracker? Because they measure different things. Average position in Search Console is the average position of your topmost result across many queries and many searchers, and Google notes that results are specific to the time, place, device and recent history of the person searching. A rank tracker checks one query from one location on a schedule. Treat them as two instruments, not two verdicts. What does it mean when a page says it is discovered but not indexed? It means Google knows the address exists and has chosen not to index it yet, or has not got to it. The usual causes are quality, duplication, thin content or a crawl decision rather than a technical block. Check for a self referencing canonical, confirm the page is linked internally, and improve the page rather than requesting indexing repeatedly. Can Search Console tell me if I have been penalised? For manual actions, yes. The Manual Actions report shows whether Google has applied one and where. It cannot show algorithmic ranking changes, which appear as gradual or abrupt declines with no notification. If traffic falls and the Manual Actions and Security Issues reports are clean, the cause is usually competitive or intent related. What should I export and keep? Keep a monthly export of the Performance report by query and by page, and a monthly count of indexed versus excluded addresses. Over two or three quarters that history is the only dependable way to tell whether a change helped, because the interface keeps only a limited window and comparisons get muddled by seasonality. Prior to partnering with Garner, lead generation was primarily managed through internal resources and direct outreach. The business identified challenges around finding qualified opportunities, limited internal resources and establishing a stronger local presence in Australia. For a business expanding its footprint in ANZ, the opportunity extended beyond lead generation alone. Updapt needed an Australian based outbound capability that could represent the business locally, engage relevant decision makers and provide genuine feedback from the market. The Garner Approach Garner worked as an extension of Updapt’s business development function, providing local outbound capability and taking the company’s ESG proposition directly to the Australian market. The campaign focused on identifying relevant organisations and decision makers , initiating meaningful conversations and creating opportunities for the Updapt team to engage directly with prospective customers. Importantly, the campaign also established a valuable feedback loop between the Australian market and Updapt. Through direct conversations with local organisations, Garner was able to provide insight into how Australian businesses were approaching ESG, their reporting priorities and how Updapt’s proposition resonated with prospective customers. This allowed the campaign to deliver value beyond outbound activity, helping Updapt test its positioning and develop a stronger understanding of local buyer behaviour. The Results Within the first one to two months, Updapt began seeing early traction from the campaign. The client reported an improvement in the quality of leads and sales conversations and highlighted the additional insight gained into Australian market needs and customer behaviour. Through the engagement, Garner helped Updapt: Establish a dedicated local outbound presence in Australia Generate quality meetings with relevant Australian prospects Create meaningful conversations with key decision makers Gain first hand insight into Australian market needs and buyer behaviour Test and refine its proposition within the local market Build a foundation of market intelligence to support future ANZ growth Extend its business development capability without immediately building an Australian outbound team internally The engagement demonstrated the value of having experienced local representation when entering and developing a new geographic market. Updapt specifically identified regional market presence for organisations yet to establish themselves in ANZ as one of the biggest areas of potential value in working with Garner. The Client Experience A key part of the engagement was Garner’s ability to operate collaboratively with the Updapt team and adapt the campaign based on feedback and market response. Updapt highlighted Garner’s team as approachable, easy to work with and receptive to feedback throughout the engagement. “Very approachable and easy to work with. The Garner team has been open to feedback and provided valuable local support as we looked to expand our presence in the Australian market.” Adapted from Updapt’s client feedback for case study use. The original feedback described Garner as approachable and easy to work with, open to feedback, and identified regional market presence as a key value. The client also confirmed they would be comfortable recommending Garner to others based on their overall experience working with the team. Looking Ahead For Updapt, partnering with Garner provided a practical way to establish an Australian outbound presence while continuing to build its understanding of the local market. Garner provided the local capability to take Updapt’s proposition directly to Australian businesses, engage relevant decision makers and turn those conversations into actionable market intelligence. Through targeted outreach and local representation, the campaign generated quality meetings while giving Updapt greater visibility into how Australian organisations were approaching ESG and sustainability requirements. Beyond lead generation, the partnership provided Updapt with an experienced local presence to support its expansion into the Australian market without the immediate need to build an internal sales development function. The engagement reinforced an important part of Garner’s offering: helping international businesses establish a local presence, test their proposition and accelerate their expansion into the Australian and broader ANZ market. Berlin-based spend management platform Moss raises capital Germany has a new fintech unicorn. Moss , a spend management platform based in Berlin, has raised €30 million ($35 million) in Series C funding. The round was led by Portage and Cherry Ventures. It brings the company’s total funding to more than €200 million ($234 million) and gives the firm a valuation of more than €1 billion. The funding will enable Moss to develop additional AI agents to automate financial processes for small and medium-sized companies. “This round reflects the trust of customers and partners in shaping the future of finance,” Moss CEO and Co-Founder Ante Spittler said in a LinkedIn post announcing the investment. “It allows us to expand beyond spend management and further build out our Finance AI product suite. Soon, Moss will allow customers to configure agents for every finance job while maintaining full control over every step and decision taken. This is Finance AI, shaped by you.” Founded in 2019 by Spittler, Anton Rummel, Ferdinand Meyer, and Stephan Haslebacher, Moss was among the first fintechs to offer corporate credit cards to German startups. Today, the company combines corporate cards, invoice management, reimbursements, real-time budgeting, and automated accounting in a single platform. Moss leverages agentic AI to automatically categorize and reconcile transactions and reports that its AI agents process more than two million transactions a month. The investment also paves the way for Moss’ development of what the company and investor Cherry Ventures refer to as Finance AI: “AI that prepares the work, shows its reasoning down to the ledger account, and takes no consequential action without the team’s sign-off,” Cherry Ventures noted in a LinkedIn post. “Moss asked its customers what they wanted from AI and built exactly that, control at every step.” Cherry Ventures was referring to a Moss survey that indicated that 48% of financial leaders identified “control” as their top priority when it came to deploying AI, with only 6% wanting AI to have “full autonomy.” Moss serves more than 5,000 businesses and generates more than €70 million in annual revenue. In addition to its Berlin headquarters, the company has offices in Tallinn and Amsterdam. YouLend partners with comrce on embedded capital Embedded finance platform YouLend and e-commerce software platform for German SMEs comrce have forged a strategic partnership to help small businesses access working capital directly from within their current e-commerce operations. The partnership will combine comrce’s e-commerce platform with YouLend’s embedded finance technology to enable Germany’s 24,000 merchants to explore potential financing options. “With YouLend, we are expanding our e-commerce offering with a service that can support merchants as they take their next steps towards growth,” comrce Head of Partner Management Amirah Hadry said. YouLend and comrce have been partners since May, but are just now formally announcing their alliance. The partnership will make information about YouLend financing options available alongside the software and communications channels used by merchants to manage orders, inventory, accounting, and customer service. comrce will direct merchant financing queries to YouLend, which manages the financing process via its digital platform. “comrce is part of the day-to-day operations of around 24,000 merchants,” YouLend General Manager Europe Leonard Strigel said. “Now, we are bringing them flexible financing options to give them greater access to growth capital. Our partnership demonstrates how embedded financing is incredibly vital to the day-to-day success of small businesses.” Founded in 2015 and headquartered in the UK, YouLend offers an embedded financing platform that powers e-commerce, payments, and technology firms ranging from Amazon to SumUp. The company operates in more than 11 markets across the UK, EU, and US. A leading e-commerce software hub, comrce offers specialized e-commerce solutions such as Billbee (automated order processing), Amainvoice (accounting software), Replyco (e-commerce helpdesk), and VentoryOne (inventory management) from a single location. Headquartered in Twistetal, Germany, and founded in 2023, comrce gives retailers an integrated ecosystem for automation, multichannel management, and revenue optimization. N26 integrates with Instant Payments System Wero Berlin-based neobank N26 has unveiled its support for Wero , the new pan-European instant payment system, via its mobile app. The launch makes the payment service available to eligible customers in Germany and France, with a gradual rollout to other markets planned for the future. N26 joined the payment system in December 2025, entering into a strategic collaboration that has culminated in the August launch. Embedding Wero into the N26 app’s native transfer flow will enable users to benefit from a single European payment standard for daily digital transactions. The integration will allow users to send and receive funds instantly with individuals who do not hold an N26 account without requiring bank details or an additional app. Transfers are powered by SEPA Instant and the Wero network and arrive in the recipient’s account in less than 10 seconds. “Instant payments without an IBAN have been a core N26 feature since our inception,” N26 Chief Product and Business Officer Daniel Lappas said. “With Wero, we’re extending this seamless experience to the broader European banking ecosystem, bringing the simplicity N26 customers already know to even more people.” A European digital bank with a German banking license, N26 offers secure, digital-native banking to millions of customers across 24 markets. Founded in 2013, N26 offers bank accounts, debit cards, international transfers, savings and investments, and insurance products. Today, the bank holds more than €10.5 billion in customer deposits and reported annual revenue of more than €500 million in 2025, marking the firm’s first full year of net profitability. N26 started the year with the launch of its N26 for under 18s solution, a debit card designed for children aged 7 to 17 and managed via their parent’s N26 app. Here is our look at fintech innovation around the world. Analysis Berlin-based fintech startup mika has successfully closed a €6 million seed funding round, signaling a significant push to automate and simplify accounting and tax processes for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Germany. The company aims to fundamentally alter the necessity of traditional tax advisors for limited liability companies, a move that could reshape the professional services sector for millions of businesses. The funding round was led by Smedvig Ventures , with participation from notable investors including the Basel-based family office Wecken & Cie. , studiVZ co-founders Dennis Bemmann and Michael Brehm , limango founder Johannes Ditterich , and encourageventures ' Martina Pfeifer . Existing backers Keen Venture Partners and Dutch Founders Fund also increased their stakes, underscoring strong confidence in mika 's vision and execution. Germany presents a particularly challenging market for accounting and tax compliance due to its intricate regulations and the direct impact of errors on tax liabilities. mika 's core innovation lies in its AI-native general ledger, designed to interpret financial documents and transactions with minimal human intervention. The platform leverages a suite of specialized AI models, integrated with proprietary industry expertise and rule sets, to automate categorization, booking, and explanation of financial data. This approach aims to significantly reduce the burden and cost associated with mandatory bookkeeping, VAT pre-declarations, and annual financial statements for the nearly one million small capital companies operating in the country. Agnieszka Walorska , co-founder and CEO of mika , highlighted the systemic barriers faced by new entrepreneurs, particularly those without access to capital or established networks. "The assumption that every German GmbH needs a tax advisor is so ingrained that many founders believe it's a legal mandate. This isn't the case, and it creates a significant hurdle, especially for individuals from less privileged backgrounds," Walorska stated. mika 's mission is to democratize access to essential financial management tools, ensuring that financial obligations do not disproportionately disadvantage aspiring business owners. Currently, over 750 companies utilize mika 's platform, a substantial increase from around 400 at the beginning of the year. While initially focused on digital service providers like agencies and consultancies, the user base has expanded to include sectors such as SaaS, real estate, e-commerce, retail, and trades. The company reports impressive revenue growth, exceeding 20 percent month-over-month for several consecutive months. Although mika handles the bulk of accounting tasks, a team of trained accountants provides oversight and handles complex cases, while the platform also facilitates direct interaction with users' financial data through AI assistants via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Freddie Kalfayan , Principal at Smedvig Ventures , commented on the market opportunity, noting that Germany's accounting and tax system is among the most complex and costly in Europe for small businesses.
